text: I remember standing on the roof that night.
Please remember to check the date before you file.
She stopped to look at the tanks.
She stopped looking at the tanks.
Here is the embarrassing part. I remember filing that story the same night. I would have sworn to it. The notebook says I filed it two days later.
So the memory was not just wrong, it was self-serving. Two days makes you slower, and less heroic.
Exactly. Which is why I stopped trusting the version I remember and went back to the paper.
Do you regret writing the book at all? Some people would have left that night alone.
No. What I regret is not checking my own notes sooner. I went on to rewrite three chapters once I did.
Then why keep the mistake in? You could simply have stopped to correct the dates and moved on.
Because the mistake is the most honest thing in the book. It shows how a memory improves a story, given enough time.
So the book owns up to the error and keeps it on display. That rings truer than a clean version would.
I remember standing on the roof, and I have never regretted staying.
I regret to say that I defended the piece for ten minutes.
She did not stop to argue. She stopped me instead.
I meant to answer her, and I could not.
This book is an attempt to stop improving the story.

People ask me whether I kept a diary in those years, and the honest answer is that I tried to keep one and gave up after a month. What I have instead are notebooks, and the notebooks are humbling. I remember writing certain sentences, word for word, and when I go back to the page, the sentence is not there. Something else is there, flatter and more careful. So I stopped trusting my memory of the notebooks and started trusting the notebooks themselves, which is harder than it sounds, because the notebooks are less flattering. The memory has had thirty years to improve the story. The page has not. If there is a rule I follow in the book, it is this one: where the two disagree, the page wins, and I say so in the text.

I read memoirs for a living, and I would ask you to read them the way a historian does, which is gratefully and suspiciously at the same time. Gratefully, because a memoir records what nobody else was in a position to see: the mood in a room, the hour at which a decision was really made. Suspiciously, because every memoir is written by the one person with the strongest interest in how the story ends. Notice which mistakes the author owns up to. They are almost always the small, forgivable ones. The large ones tend to be described in the passive voice, or not at all. And when a writer says they regret not having said something at the time, ask yourself why they are saying it now, and to whom.
